newsitem.title: GERMANY: German bank sector starts talks on sick pay row.
newsitem.headline: German bank sector starts talks on sick pay row.

text.p: German bank employers and trade unions began talks on Monday aimed at resolving a dispute over the decision by major German banks to cut sick pay entitlements in accordance with a controversial new law.

Gerhard Renner, chief negotiator for the white-collar union DAG, warned before the talks in Frankfurt, Germany's banking centre, that there would be protests across the sector as early as this week if the banks did not back down from the cuts.

Last month more than 15,000 German bank employees took to the streets to protest against a 20 percent cut made to sick payments by most of the major commercial banks including Deutsche Bank, the country's largest.

The banking sector is the only large industry in Germany where employers have acted together to enforce the law, which was part of an austerity package introduced by Bonn to ensure German entry to the single European currency in 1999.

In the large metal and engineering industries, many employers are largely resigned to the fact that huge worker resistance has made the cuts unenforceable, while other sectors such as the chemical industry have postponed a decision.

Germany's banks have so far said they have been little affected by industrial action by bank workers, which has been relatively limited compared to protests involving hundreds of thousands of engineering workers.

But the worsening of relations in the German banking sector, which has not seen widespread industrial action since 1992, comes as the major banks are seeking to win more business by extending opening hours.
That is expected to mean requiring employees to work more overtime -- something that many bank staff are already refusing to do as a result of the cuts to sick pay.

But bank employers say that, unlike some contracts in the metal and engineering sector, wage contracts for bank workers do not specifically protect sick pay at 100 percent of salary and therefore they are free to impose the cuts.
Bank unions argue on the other hand that the low absenteeism in the sector makes the potential savings from the cuts insignificant.
